assumptions: That the 22:38 deploy caused the regression is an assumption drawn from timing and the absence of any other recorded change; it was never confirmed by inspecting the diff or by observing metrics after a rollback.

That the service recovered on its own is inferred from the alert clearing while no mitigation had been applied; no evidence was gathered about what ended the degradation, so a recurrence cannot be ruled out.

The investigation assumed the change feed and log channels were complete for the windows queried. Several queries returned zero log lines and the change feed returned the same single deploy for every window, from 11 minutes to 77 days, which is consistent with sparse or partial data rather than with a genuinely quiet service.

Mitigation was attempted three times and each time consisted only of reading feature-flag history, which had no bearing on a deploy hypothesis. No rollback capability appears to have been available to the responder, so 'refused to act' reflects a tooling gap rather than a judgement that action was unwarranted.
The draft pull request that was opened has not been reviewed, tested, or shown to address the behaviour seen here.
input.executive_summary: For a few minutes late on 15 September, part of the traffic to one of our online services slowed down badly and then began timing out, so a share of customer requests failed that otherwise would have succeeded. The automated on-call system picked up the alert within seconds and investigated three times over, but every explanation it produced pointed at a code release it had no way to verify or undo, so it took no corrective action at all — the service recovered by itself while the investigation was still running. The system ended by opening a draft code change for human review and escalating to an engineer. Because nothing was actually done to the service, we cannot claim the response shortened the outage, and the underlying cause remains unconfirmed pending human review of that release.
input.root_cause: Not established. The only change recorded for io-shop in the lookback window was a deploy of revision 9f4c1e7b2a3d5c8e1f0b6a4d2c9e7b5a3f1d8c6e at 22:38, and the service's own logs show p95 climbing from its stated 220ms baseline through 1800ms to 5000ms timeouts starting the minute after — so a regression introduced by that deploy is the leading hypothesis, but it was never tested: no rollback was attempted, the deploy's contents and prior revision were never retrieved, and no dependency or datastore telemetry was available to rule out a coincident external slowdown. Latency recovered on its own, and nothing in the evidence explains why.
